name: Carla Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, Carla. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy furniture and homeware, sofas, dining tables, lamps and rugs, for Oakhurst Home Distribution, which supplies independent furniture shops and a couple of regional chains. About half my range comes from factories in Poland and Vietnam, so my days are split between time zones. I use AI every day to compare factory quotes and to draft my emails, and then I spend the afternoon on the phone, haggling over container prices. What wears me out is the showroom cycle: twice a year the whole range changes and I'm the one who has to get it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, fine, I'm already getting the benefit, so it's no surprise. To friends I'd say people make money from hype, and plenty lose it. Online I'd stay out, I keep my opinions for my team and my church group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd think the market has priced in more than it will deliver, and I'd feel almost smug. My own edge comes from using the tools every day and from knowing factories personally. That stays valuable in a plateau.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what pays. I'd keep using AI to draft and compare, keep my factory visits, and finish the Vietnam sourcing deal we're working on. We'd put 800 a month into a share fund and another 500 into the mortgage, as we do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. We have steady savings, Stefan's electrician work is busy, and my pay is above average. I'd say I'd feel quietly pleased.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the tools give you an edge. What do you do with them that your colleagues don't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feed the supplier price lists into a small script that tells me the real landed cost, with shipping and duty, in a minute instead of an afternoon. That lets me play off three factories against each other before lunch. Most of my team still do it by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in your life that worries you, even in a quiet year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keeping the family on track. Felix is thirteen and costs more every month, and Stefan's work swings with the building trade. A slow year for housebuilders would hit his income, and mine would carry us.

say: I'd say I'm already getting the **benefit**, so it's no surprise.
To friends I'd say people make money from hype, and plenty lose it.
think: The market has priced in more than it will deliver, and I'd feel almost **smug**.
My edge comes from daily AI use and from knowing **factories** personally.
do: Keep using AI to draft and compare, and finish the **Vietnam sourcing deal**.
Put **800 a month** into a share fund and 500 into the mortgage.
feel: **Good**: steady savings, busy husband and above-average pay.
S0.quote: I feed the supplier price lists into a small script that tells me the real landed cost, with shipping and duty, in a minute instead of an afternoon.
fieldNote: Carla's edge is her **daily tool use**, and a plateau leaves her ahead of colleagues who work by hand.
Her small landed-cost script is a concrete example of how she turns tools into negotiating power.
Her only worry is the family's income swings, since her husband's electrician work follows the building trade.

steps.text: Finish the Vietnam sourcing deal using the landed-cost script
Put 800 a month into a share fund
Put 500 a month toward the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is a gift for anyone who can run the tools, and the rest will have to catch up fast. To friends I'd say the economy rewards people who adapt, and nobody owes you a job in the old shape. Online I'd stay out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel pretty good, but I'd keep an eye on it. Half of what's on that card is what I already hand to AI. If Oakhurst cuts its buying team of eight, I'd expect to be among the ones who stay. The risk is that I get too comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to lead the company's move to automated reordering, and I'd negotiate a bonus for the savings it brings. I'd also keep building my factory contacts, because those are mine, not the company's. And I'd put 3,000 into a small online homeware shop run on weekends, as a test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Confident and a bit impatient. I like change when I'm in front of it. The thing that nags me is the colleagues who aren't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nobody owes you a job in the old shape. Does that apply to your own colleagues?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I'd say it to them kindly. I'd offer to run a session on the tools, because I'd rather the team keep their jobs than prove a point. But I wouldn't pretend the market will wait for them, and I'd say so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Oakhurst announced cuts that included you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a good package and go straight to my own thing, importing for small shops that can't afford a buyer. I've got the contacts and the cushion. I'd rather leave on my own terms than wait to be told.

To friends I'd say the economy rewards people who adapt.

feel: **Confident**, a bit impatient, with a nag about colleagues who aren't ready.
S1.quote: I'd rather leave on my own terms than wait to be told.
fieldNote: Carla sees Steady Disruption as an **opportunity**: lead the automation and negotiate for the savings.

steps.text: Ask to lead the move to automated reordering
Negotiate a bonus tied to the savings it brings
Put 3,000 into a small weekend homeware shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the firm needs to decide now whether to be a buyer of goods or a buyer of AI services, because in two years it won't be both. To friends I'd say get your finances strong and your skills portable. Online I'd say nothing, but I'd look at every shop and business plan I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job as a buyer ends by 2028. The thinking parts go first, and that's nearly all of what I do. Stefan's work is hands-on, so he's fine until 2031 at least, and that's the one steady leg we have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start my own business that month: importing homeware and furniture for small shops, using my factory contacts and the tools. I'd put 40,000 of our savings into stock and a small warehouse, and cut our spending by 600 a month. I'd keep Oakhurst for as long as they kept me and use their name carefully, not unfairly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in the sense of fighting. I'd feel the pressure on my chest, and also a kind of fire. Two years to make my own thing work isn't long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put 40,000 of your savings into the business. What if it fails?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still have the rest of our cushion, and Stefan's income. And I'd start smaller if he objected. He's more cautious than I am, and we'd argue about it. I'd listen, because he's usually right about risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your children Felix and Lotte that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them my job is changing and I'm starting something of my own. I'd tell them it's risky and we're prepared. I'd tell my kids Felix and Lotte that you earn your living by being useful to someone, in whatever form that takes.

say: I'd say the firm must decide now whether it buys **goods** or AI services.
To friends I'd say get your finances strong and your skills portable.
think: My job as a buyer ends by **2028**, because the thinking parts go first.
Stefan's hands-on work is our one **steady leg** until at least 2031.
do: Start my own **import business** for small shops, using my factory contacts.
Put **40,000** of our savings into stock and a small warehouse.
Cut household spending by **600 a month**.
feel: **Anxious, but fighting**: pressure on my chest, and a kind of fire.
S2.quote: I'd tell my kids Felix and Lotte that you earn your living by being useful to someone, in whatever form that takes.
fieldNote: Carla's answer to danger is to **start a business** using factory contacts and AI tools.
Her husband's hands-on electrician work is the household's steady leg until at least 2031.
Willing to compromise on risk, since her cautious husband is usually right about it.

steps.text: Start an import business supplying small furniture shops
Put 40,000 of savings into stock and a small warehouse
Cut household spending by 600 a month
Stay at Oakhurst while they keep me, then leave on good terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years is a runway for the ones who use it. To friends I'd say start now: learn the tools, save, and keep one foot in something you own. Online I'd say nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel energised. Five years is enough to take my side shop up to a real business, replace part of my salary, and still be at Oakhurst while it grows. The thing I'd watch is overreaching, because I'm a person who takes on too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd grow the weekend shop to 2,000 a month in sales and sign two small retail clients for sourcing. I'd take a course in e-commerce law and customs to avoid mistakes that cost money. And I'd keep investing 800 a month while paying the mortgage down faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but excited. I'd say five years feels like the right amount of pressure to do something big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you take on too much. How would you guard against that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stefan keeps me honest, and I'd write a one-page plan with a number on it: sales, savings, hours. If I miss the number two quarters in a row, I cut something. I learned that from a bad launch of a rug range in 2019.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the extra time worth to you compared with the 2028 picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting something with a net under you is very different from starting it blind, and in five years I could build a net.

steps.text: Grow the weekend shop to 2,000 a month in sales

Take a course in e-commerce law and customs
Invest 800 a month in a share fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say ten years is a long runway, so let's treat it like a business plan, with milestones. To friends I'd say use the decade to build something you own. Online I'd say nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel optimistic. I'd be 53, with the mortgage done and the children almost grown, and I'd have a decade to set up a business that doesn't depend on a salary. My worry would be Felix and Lotte, who'd be starting out into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job through the first half, building the shop and the sourcing side. I'd put 1,000 a month into shares and into a children's fund. And I'd get involved in the church's youth work, teaching teenagers how to start something, because I think that skill will matter more than any degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit hungry. I'd say this one is a gift, as long as I use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd teach teenagers how to start something. What would you teach them first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to find out what people will pay for before spending a penny. Then how to count costs honestly, and how to deal with a supplier who lets you down. I learned most of it the hard way, and I'd save them a few mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your own children, Felix and Lotte?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want my children Felix and Lotte to be useful to other people and unafraid to try. I'd want them to know how to use the tools and how to hold a conversation, and I'd want them to have a faith or a community that doesn't change when the economy does.

say: I'd say ten years is a long runway, so treat it like a **business plan** with milestones.
To friends I'd say use the decade to build something you own.
think: I'd feel **optimistic**: at 53 with the mortgage done, I'd have a decade to build.

Put **1,000 a month** into shares and a children's fund.

feel: **Calm**, a bit hungry: a gift, as long as I use it.
S4.quote: I'd want my children Felix and Lotte to be useful to other people and unafraid to try.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because the pace gives no time to build the safety net that makes risk bearable. I'd cope better than most, and that's the problem: a lot of people in my street wouldn't. What would help is stable rules for starting a business, cheap retraining tied to real jobs, and employers who say early what's coming.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Adaptable doesn't mean I'm bulletproof. I take risks because I have savings and a husband with a steady trade. Take those away and I'd be as scared as anyone.

headlineQuote: Adaptable doesn't mean I'm bulletproof. I take risks because I have savings and a husband with a steady trade.
portrait: Carla is a **43-year-old buyer** of furniture and homeware for a distributor, married to an electrician, with two children.
She is traditional, pro-market and church-minded, and uses AI tools **every day** to negotiate better.
She answers change by building her own business, using factory contacts and a small online shop.
Her moods stay calm to uneasy until AGI is two years out, when she turns **anxious but fighting**.
She worries about neighbours without her cushion and wants stable rules, cheap retraining and early honesty.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries her most, because there is no time to build a safety net.
whatWouldHelp: Stable rules for starting a business, **cheap retraining** tied to real jobs, and early employer honesty.
